concept.name: Overfitting
concept.definition: The production of a model that corresponds too closely to the particular training data, fitting noise as if it were structure, so it performs well in-sample but fails to generalize to new data. It arises whenever the selection criterion (training performance) diverges from the evaluation criterion (out-of-sample performance).
concept.intuition: The model memorizes the textbook's answers instead of learning the subject: perfect on past questions, helpless on new ones.
concept.mechanics: Risk grows with model complexity relative to data, weak signal-to-noise, and repeated reuse of the same data for tuning. Countermeasures include holdout test sets and cross-validation, regularization (ridge, lasso), early stopping, complexity penalties (AIC/BIC), and in trading walk-forward testing with trial-adjusted performance metrics.
concept.failure_modes: In-sample fit statistics (R-squared, backtest Sharpe) are upward-biased estimates of real performance, with the bias largest exactly where the search was most intense, and validation sets consulted repeatedly become training data.
concept.misconceptions: That overfitting requires huge models: three parameters mined across thousands of specification choices overfit as surely as a million-parameter network, because overfitting lives in the selection process, not just model size.
concept.example: A degree-20 polynomial threads through all 20 noisy training points with zero error yet predicts wildly off-trend on the next observation.

citations.source: scikit-learn User Guide, Section 3.1 Cross-validation: evaluating estimator performance
